transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-10-16
- Start time (UTC): 21:00
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Verdant CISO), Marcus Liu (Platform Eng), Priya Rao (SRE), Jun Park (Security Architect)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete):
Verdant Labs is evaluating Redwood's admin activity capture and export for forensic readiness. Primary asks: what admin actions are captured (role changes, token/key operations, model access), export formats (NDJSON/JSON, syslog, Kinesis/Kafka, customer-owned S3), retention tiers and pricing, and options for customer-managed encryption keys (BYOK/HSM). Discussed SOC 2 evidence needs and ISO controls mapping. Next steps: share evidence pack, sample export, and pilot scheduling.

Topics:
- Admin event types captured (user auth, RBAC changes, key rotations)
- Export & streaming (S3, Kafka, Kinesis, syslog, webhook)
- Retention policy presets + long-term archival (S3 glacier, WORM)
- Encryption and KMS/BYOK/HSM integration
- Data residency and regional export endpoints
- Forensic readiness and immutable logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: alright good afternoon everyone thanks for joining uh from Redwood side we have Diego and Nina with me, quick intros?
[00:12] Laura Kim: hi all I'm Laura kim CISO at Verdant Labs, thanks, we wanna make sure our audit trails are investigation ready for incident response and for SOC audits.
[00:20] Diego Martinez: thanks laura, can you give a quick snapshot of your current stack where you land logs today? like SIEM, S3, any streamers?
[00:28] Marcus Liu: sure we ingest into Splunk right now for most infra, and platform events go to an internal kafka cluster, we also do long-term cold storage in an aws s3 bucket zipped ndjson.
[00:38] Priya Rao: and retention for security events is typically 3 years for some teams, but ops keeps 90 days by default, so we'd like clarity on tiering.
[00:46] Avery Chen: makes sense; the goal today is to show what Redwood captures natively for admin and control-plane activity, and how we can push those artifacts to your SIEM or a customer-owned bucket with encryption controls.
[00:56] Jun Park: quick question up front, does Redwood record prompt/response pairs by default in admin logs or is that considered separate telemetry?
[01:05] Diego Martinez: good call out — by default we do not include PII/plain prompt/response payloads in admin audit exports. Admin logs capture meta-events: api key creation/deletion, token issuance, role grants and revocations, user sessions/login attempts, admin console actions (policy changes, model pinning, rollout events), model version uploads and deploy events, and service account operations. There is an optional debug mode that can capture more detailed traces but that's off by default and requires explicit consent and retention policies.
[01:37] Laura Kim: so forensics, we need immutable timelines. can you support WORM or write-once archival for evidence?
[01:44] Diego Martinez: yes - for archival we recommend delivering ndjson exports to a customer-owned S3 bucket with server-side encryption using your KMS (BYOK) and bucket immutability settings enabled. Redwood can sign and push daily/real-time files. We also support streaming via Kafka or Amazon Kinesis for near real-time ingestion — those streams are gzipped newline-delimited json (ndjson) events.
[02:05] Marcus Liu: does the stream include a monotonic event id or sequence number to reassemble causality? that helps in our SIEM correlation.
[02:12] Nina Patel: we include event_id, event_type, timestamp (ISO8601), actor (user id/email), target resource, action, request_id and an optional context blob (limited size). The sequence is available per-shard in the stream — small caveat, if we do cross-shard ordering we add a request-level causal_id to assist reassembly.
[02:33] Priya Rao: what about administrator impersonation or delegated admin events? we need to know who acted and on-behalf-of information.
[02:40] Diego Martinez: yes those are captured as separate events: impersonation_start, impersonation_end, and every admin action includes actor_type and if applicable acted_for fields.
[02:48] Laura Kim: about encryption — we need to use our keys. can you do BYOK with HSM backed keys and rotate keys on our cadence?
[02:56] Avery Chen: short answer yes, we support customer-managed keys in AWS KMS and Azure Key Vault for hosted and dedicated; on Private you can plug in your HSM. Key rotation is supported but note that rotation requires re-encryption of archived blobs if you request rewrap; for streaming to your S3 using your KMS the objects are encrypted at rest per your key policy.
[03:16] Jun Park: any limitation on log size or rate for exports? we can have bursts during incident when a retained model is storming.
[03:23] Diego Martinez: we have throttles per account but you can enable burst capacity or dedicated log-export workers as part of Dedicated plan. For hosted customers we provide SLAs and recommended ingest rates; for high-volume forensic exports we often recommend a dedicated stream or pushing to customer owned infra.
[03:38] Marcus Liu: format question — can we get a compress-and-chunk format like ndjson+gzip and partition per day? that's our preference.
[03:45] Nina Patel: absolutely. default daily rollover is available, and we can also do hourly chunking for high throughput. Filenames include UTC date and shard id, and archives are gzipped. We also supply a manifest file for integrity checks.
[03:58] Priya Rao: audit retention — what's your default and can we configure multiple tiers? legal might ask 7 years for some logs.
[04:06] Diego Martinez: default admin-event retention in Redwood Hosted is 90 days hot; you can configure extended retention to 1 year or up to 7 years via long-term archival to S3/GCS with lifecycle rules. Pricing differs — we'll share the tier sheet. Important: retention applies to what Redwood retains in our service; if you push to customer storage the retention is governed by your bucket lifecycle.
[04:29] Laura Kim: do you provide an evidence package for SOC2 audits that maps events to CC6 controls?
[04:35] Avery Chen: yes we have an evidence bundle and mapping doc that connects captured events to SOC2/ISO clauses — we'll attach the artifact. We also include sample queries and saved views for auditors.
[04:45] Jun Park: how about access control for the audit exports? we need strict IAM on the export role and minimum privilege, and the ability to revoke export keys quickly.
[04:54] Diego Martinez: exports can be done using short-lived credentials, pre-signed URLs, or cross-account IAM roles. We recommend cross-account role with least privilege; you can revoke the role or rotate the trust relationship immediately. For Kafka we support mTLS and ACLs.
[05:08] Priya Rao: is there an option to stream to syslog or a Splunk HEC endpoint? that's what our infra team likes.
[05:15] Nina Patel: yes — syslog over TLS or Splunk HEC are supported; events map to a schema we provide. Some transformations may be necessary for field names, we'll provide a mapper script.
[05:26] Marcus Liu: any PII concerns? we need to ensure user identifiers in logs are pseudonymized or reversible only by our team.
[05:33] Diego Martinez: by default we include user_id and email hashed/pseudonymized on request. For compliance we can provide a reversible encryption using your KMS for certain fields, but that adds complexity to retrieval and key management — usually customers choose hashing for general audit and reversible encryption for legal holds.
[05:56] Laura Kim: on the legal hold topic: can we do hold flags so that certain objects are not purged by lifecycle rules?
[06:02] Avery Chen: yes, when logs are pushed to your S3 with your KMS you can enable S3 Object Lock (WORM) and legal hold. Redwood will not delete objects that are under lock if they're in your bucket — if logs are retained in Redwood-managed storage we can apply similar immutability windows per contract for Dedicated/Private.
[06:18] Marcus Liu: are there alerts if export fails? we need SLA monitoring and retries.
[06:22] Diego Martinez: we emit export_status events and will retry; we also have an alerting webhook you can subscribe to, plus console metrics per-route and per-export. For critical pipelines we recommend a mirrored stream for redundancy.
[06:36] Priya Rao: curious about what is considered admin 'action' granularity — do you capture policy diffs or just the end-state?
[06:43] Nina Patel: we capture policy change events including the diff payload and who submitted it, plus previous hash for audit. Full diff stored in archival mode; in hot logs we store a brief summary and a reference to the archived diff.
[06:57] Laura Kim: ok that helps. for our internal change review board we need both the diff and the approval chain. can you annotate events with approver information?
[07:05] Diego Martinez: yes we can surface approval metadata when integrated with your ticketing or approval system via connectors — will take some mapping work, we can prototype in the pilot.
[07:17] Jun Park: let me ask a tricky one — do you capture model inference metadata that might be considered sensitive e.g., if a user uploads PII within a prompt is there leakage into audit traces?
[07:27] Diego Martinez: we avoid capturing payloads in audit trails by default. If you enable debug tracing you can capture more but it should be treated as sensitive and forwarded only to your encrypted storage. We also have a redact-at-ingest pipeline that can mask PII fields before writing them to exports.
[07:46] Marcus Liu: retention/ingest pricing ballpark? we need to justify long-term storage cost to finance.
[07:51] Avery Chen: we'll send you the tiered pricing spreadsheet — short answer: hot retention is priced per GB-month in platform; archival to customer S3 offloads that cost (you pay storage) but there are charges for egress/processing. We'll include a sample cost calc for 1TB/month of logs.
[08:06] Laura Kim: for SOC2 evidence we may need export snapshots at auditor request. can you generate point-in-time export packages and a signed manifest?
[08:14] Nina Patel: yes, we can produce signed manifests (SHA256) and bundle exports for the requested timeframe; these are suitable for auditor ingestion.
[08:22] Priya Rao: are there any known gaps relative to ISO 27001 control families? I want to surface anything we should watch.
[08:30] Diego Martinez: generally we have coverage for audit logging, access control, key management, and incident response. Items that sometimes need extra customer work: integrating existing SIEM backward compatibility, ticketing/approval integration, and legal hold workflows which depend on your cloud provider capabilities. We'll include a mapping doc.
[08:49] Laura Kim: ok let's talk next steps — who owns what?
[08:53] Avery Chen: action items we've captured: we'll send security artifacts and evidence pack, Diego will produce sample exports + mapping, and Marcus will share endpoints and IAM contact. We'll schedule a pilot where we stream to the customer-owned S3/Kafka and run a small simulation.
[09:08] Jun Park: one more small note — for our compliance we prefer EU residency for log storage. can you confirm regional endpoints for log export?
[09:15] Nina Patel: yes, we have region-specific export endpoints (eu-west-1, us-west-2, ap-southeast-1) and can ensure data egress stays within region when set in customer's org config. We'll include that in the setup doc.
[09:28] Marcus Liu: great, that's all from platform.
[09:31] Laura Kim: thanks everyone appreciate the detail. please include a short checklist for audit evidence that we can hand to our auditor.
[09:39] Avery Chen: will do — checklist + mapping + sample export. thanks for the time.
[09:43] (end of recording)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., sam-el -> SAML, kv cache pronounced K-V cash), speaker labels are best-effort.
